passage:
January: Nikita, a junior analyst at a Mumbai logistics firm, opened a new notebook and wrote: "Client renews contract: 90%. I get the Delhi project: 70%. Shipment arrives on time: 95%." Tanuja laughed. "You're grading yourself?" "Checking my gut," Nikita said.
April: She ticked and crossed. The client had renewed. She hadn't got Delhi. Two of four 95% shipments had been late.
July: Nikita showed Tanuja the pattern on a spreadsheet. "When I'm sure about people, I'm usually right. When I'm sure about timelines, I'm right only about half the time." She now adds a week to her delivery estimates and trusts her read on clients.

qa.q: How many of the four 95% shipments were late?
qa.a: Two of four 95% shipments had been late.

qa.q: Why did Nikita start writing percentages in a notebook?
qa.a: She wanted to test how far her sure feelings could be trusted, instead of assuming her gut was always right.

qa.q: What changed in how Nikita works after July, and why is it sensible?
qa.a: She adds a week to delivery estimates and keeps trusting her read on clients, because her own record showed timelines were where her confidence misled her.

qa.q: How might Tanuja see the notebook by July?
qa.a: Tanuja, who laughed at first, may now see it as useful, since it turned vague confidence into a clear pattern anyone could learn from.

grounding: Shows a young professional writing predictions with percentages, checking them months later and learning where her confidence is reliable.

passage: Neelam, you asked how your Gargi ma'am got so good at estimating. It wasn't talent. When I was twenty-five and new at the newspaper, I was sure of everything: which story would lead, which minister would resign, which intern would last. So my editor dared me to write each guess with a percentage in a little diary. "Page-one story: 80%." "Rain delays the match: 60%." Every month I checked. It was humbling. My 90s about politics came true barely half the time. My 70s about sports were bang on. Slowly I learned where my gut was a good friend and where it was a loud stranger. I still keep that diary. It's right here on my desk.

qa.q: What did the editor dare Gargi to do?
qa.a: The editor dared her to write each guess with a percentage in a little diary.

qa.q: How did Gargi feel when she first checked the diary?
qa.a: She felt humbled and surprised, because her confident guesses about politics came true barely half the time.

qa.q: What could Neelam start doing tomorrow, based on this story?
qa.a: Neelam could write down a few work predictions with percentages and check them every month to learn which kinds of guesses deserve trust.

qa.q: Why might Gargi's editor have suggested the diary?
qa.a: The editor probably saw a talented young reporter who was sure of everything and wanted her to learn from her own record rather than from criticism.

grounding: Shows a grounded professional who wrote predictions with percentages and checked them, learning where her sure feelings were reliable.

passage: Thunder cracked over Kochi and the wedding planner's phone buzzed nonstop. Mahima had forty minutes to decide whether to move the reception indoors. Deepak, her assistant, was panicking. "The forecast says sixty percent rain. What's your gut?" Mahima's gut said the storm would pass. But she opened the small spreadsheet she had kept for two years: every weather call she had made, how confident she had been, and what happened. Her "storm will pass" calls at around seventy percent had been right only half the time. "My gut isn't as good as it feels on weather," she said. "We move indoors." At seven the rain came down in sheets. The guests ate dry, and Deepak stopped panicking.

qa.q: How long did Mahima have to decide?
qa.a: Mahima had forty minutes to decide.

qa.q: Why didn't Mahima simply follow her gut about the storm?
qa.a: Her own records showed her confident weather calls were right only half the time, so she knew her gut felt surer than it deserved on this kind of question.

qa.q: What makes Mahima's spreadsheet useful under time pressure?
qa.a: It turns two years of past guesses into a quick check, so even with forty minutes she can see how far to trust the feeling instead of arguing with it.

qa.q: How might Deepak see Mahima after the rain came?
qa.a: Deepak would probably trust her more, seeing that she checked her own confidence instead of just sounding sure. 😊

grounding: Shows a professional using her record of past predictions and confidence levels to decide whether to trust a sure feeling under time pressure.

passage: Every Monday morning at her desk in a Hyderabad architecture office, Ayesha opened a small spreadsheet and typed three predictions. "Client approves the facade by Friday: 80%." "Structural drawings back this week: 60%." "The site visit happens on time: 90%." On the last Friday of each month she went back and marked what really happened. Her colleague Kavitha found it odd at first. "You're just guessing." "I'm checking my guesses," Ayesha said. After three months a pattern was clear. When she said 90% about her own work, she was right almost every time. But when she said 80% about clients approving things fast, she was right only about half the time. "So my sure feeling about clients is too sure," she told Kavitha. Next week, she typed, "Client approves by Friday: 55%." Then she warned the team to keep a buffer.

qa.q: On which day did Ayesha go back and mark what really happened?
qa.a: On the last Friday of each month.

qa.q: How does Ayesha seem to feel when she discovers her client predictions were too sure?
qa.a: She seems curious rather than upset, treating the result as useful information about where her confidence can and cannot be trusted.

qa.q: What change did Ayesha make after seeing the pattern, and why does it help?
qa.a: She lowered her client prediction to 55% and told the team to keep a buffer, so plans match how things usually go.

qa.q: How might Kavitha's view of the spreadsheet change over the three months?
qa.a: Kavitha first thought it was just guessing, but seeing Ayesha adjust real plans could make Kavitha see it as a smart habit.

grounding: A young architect writes predictions with percentages, checks them monthly, and learns where her confident feelings are reliable.

passage:
"Bhavna, it's Sunday. Why are you marking a notebook at breakfast?"
"It's my prediction book, Kunal. Every January I write down guesses with percentages."
Her brother leaned over. "'Get the Pune account: 90%.' Did you?"
"Yes. Tick."
"'Team wins the quarterly award: 85%.'"
"No." She drew a cross. "And look. 'Boss approves leave in first try: 80%.' Cross again."
Mummy poured the tea. "So your feeling is wrong?"
"Not always. When it's about my own clients, I'm usually right. When it depends on other people's decisions, I'm too sure."
Kunal laughed. "So you're overconfident about everyone else."
"About guessing what they'll do, yes. Next year I'll put those lower."
"Can I start one?" Kunal asked.
"Only if you check it in December."

qa.q: What was Bhavna's prediction about the Pune account?
qa.a: Get the Pune account: 90%.

qa.q: How does Bhavna feel about the crosses in her book?
qa.a: She seems calm and interested rather than embarrassed, because the crosses show her exactly where her confidence is too high.

qa.q: What does Bhavna decide to do differently next year, and why?
qa.a: She will give lower percentages to predictions that depend on other people's decisions, because her checks show she is too sure about those.

qa.q: Why might Kunal want to start his own prediction book?
qa.a: Seeing his sister learn something useful about herself from ticks and crosses makes the habit look practical and a bit fun.

grounding: At a family breakfast, a young woman checks her yearly percentage predictions and finds where her confidence is and isn't reliable.
